Prompt:
A translator of a coastal diary kept an unfamiliar word for the basket in which a fisher carried the day's catch. Her editor proposed simply “basket.” In defense of the original word the translator described its close weave, the curl of its handle, its tendency to list on an uneven deck. The editor replied that every basket in every language has a shape, and that a catalogue of shapes is not a diary. Both assumed that the word's work could be settled by inspecting the object. Yet later in the diary the same word is spoken to a son who has announced his departure. His father says only, “Take the basket.” By then the family has sold its boat. If the reader has had to pause at this word before, the father's remark may recall mornings of shared work. If the reader has paused at a dozen unexplained words on each page, it may recall only the difficulty of the translation. The translator's choice therefore depends partly on a resource that no dictionary lists: the attention she has already asked her reader to spend.

What resource limits the translator’s ability to make a particular unfamiliar word memorable?
Answer: The reader's remaining attention for unfamiliar language.
Reason: The author presents a pause as meaningful when it is distinctive and tiring when repeated indiscriminately.
Source: AAMC, What's on the MCAT exam? Framework for original practice · https://students-residents.aamc.org/prepare-mcat-exam/whats-mcat-exam-pdf-outline · Original passage and three independently graded questions

Prompt:
A city considered removing a row of benches outside its railway station. In six weeks of observation, its consultant recorded a seated occupant in only one of every ten scans. The consultant's arithmetic was impeccable. A shopkeeper, asked whether the benches were useful, answered by pointing to a woman standing at the timetable. Before the benches appeared, she said, the woman would have waited inside the shop, where a place to rest was assured. The woman had never actually sat on a bench. A councillor treated the story as an attempt to substitute sentiment for counting. That criticism goes too far. The story suggests a second count one might make: how often people who need occasional rest now choose the route past the station. It provides no count of its own, and the shopkeeper might have misread a customer's motives. Still, a measure cannot earn authority over an entire question merely by being more exact than the alternatives. Its authority extends to the thing it measures. Empty benches are excellent evidence about occupancy and rather less decisive evidence about what a street allows.

What does the author accept about the consultant’s result?
Answer: It accurately describes observed bench occupancy.
Reason: The dispute concerns the inference about usefulness.
Source: AAMC, What's on the MCAT exam? Framework for original practice · https://students-residents.aamc.org/prepare-mcat-exam/whats-mcat-exam-pdf-outline · Original passage and three independently graded questions

Prompt:
The village clock was a poor instrument by the time the council voted to preserve it. Its minute hand sometimes gained in damp weather and sometimes lost in dry. The engineer who examined it warned that no ordinary repair would make it reliable enough to govern the departure of a train. This alarmed the councillors until somebody noticed that no train had departed from the village for thirty years. After that the engineer’s report was quoted as though it had proved that the clock had no use at all. Its defenders responded in the same spirit. They claimed that every family planned its day by the chimes. A week spent asking families would have relieved them of this attractive belief.

One baker offered a more modest account. She set her ovens by a cheap electric timer. What the old clock gave her, she said, was a moment in the afternoon when the people outside her door looked up together. A visitor might suppose that this demonstrated the charm of an antique sound. Yet the baker had nothing kind to say about the bell itself, which had a crack and struck her as rather shrill. She was describing an arrangement among listeners. Almost any sound would have served, provided everyone knew that everyone else could hear it. A hundred accurate watches, each vibrating discreetly against a wrist, could tell the time more faithfully while doing little for that arrangement.

At this point an advocate of economy might propose a loudspeaker. The proposal deserves a more civil hearing than antiquarians usually grant it. A message broadcast daily at the same hour could indeed coordinate attention. The trouble is that an announcement has a speaker. Somebody would have to decide what the daily message said. Even if the message were simply a recorded chime, somebody could decide tomorrow that the occasion was better used for a warning about litter. The old clock could be silenced or moved, so it enjoyed no absolute immunity from officials. But its mechanism was sufficiently stubborn to make a change of subject difficult. Its limited vocabulary was part of the arrangement.

This argument supplies no general warrant for saving clocks. In a neighboring town the striking of the hour might wake night workers without creating any publicly valued moment. Nor does it establish that this village should spend whatever repair might cost. It does suggest a question that neither the engineer nor the clock’s defenders had asked. If an object appears inefficient at its stated purpose, which of its constraints have people quietly made useful? An answer may justify repair, replacement, or removal. The point of asking is to keep the easiest thing to measure from silently selecting among those options. An inventory of accurate timepieces would settle whether the baker needed help timing her ovens. It would tell us very little about what happened outside her door.

A shared use can depend on a constraint that measures of an object's stated purpose overlook.
Villages should preserve a common daily sound whenever residents own accurate watches.
A mechanical device is usually less open to political interference than a broadcast system.
Answer: A shared use can depend on a constraint that measures of an object's stated purpose overlook.
Reason: The author uses the clock to ask which constraints support an acquired use. The conclusion leaves the preservation decision open.

Prompt:
When the city archive began digitizing petitions, volunteers received a practical instruction. Copy the words that appear on the page. A volunteer who found seven nearly identical petitions from a single street entered all seven. Another, facing two hundred printed petitions signed by different hands, entered the text just once and attached a list of names. Both believed they had obeyed. Yet a historian searching for a phrase about the price of coal would retrieve seven documents from the first street and one from the second. The difference was born at a desk decades after the coal had been burned.

One proposed remedy was to count signatures. A hundred names, on this view, ought to carry the same weight whether they arrived on one sheet or a hundred. That seems fair if the historian wants to know how many people were willing to put their names to a demand. But a signature gathered during a shift change could take seconds, while delivering a petition to the council might cost a day’s wages. A signature count retains an answer about participation while discarding evidence about the work of organizing it. The two streets might have differed most in precisely that respect.

A second remedy was to preserve photographs of every sheet. The photographs were welcome. One showed that what looked in transcription like a second signer was a witness attesting to the mark of someone who could not write. Yet photographs do little for the reader who is first deciding which street to investigate. That reader still encounters a list produced by choices about what counts as a document. A picture can correct a conclusion once the reader has found it. It cannot, by itself, tell the reader which pictures the search failed to bring together.

There was a further difficulty. A husband and wife sometimes signed one sheet under the name of their shop. Counting the sheet was easy. Counting the names meant deciding whether the couple, the shop, or the person who held the pen had made the demand. Even the apparently modest unit of a participant already contained an interpretation.

Some archivists took this argument as an objection to counting. Far from it. If no one counts anything, a street represented by one eloquent letter may fill half a chapter while a street represented by forty terse petitions gets a sentence. The discipline of counting can expose that imbalance. The difficulty begins when the count is allowed to travel without its question. “Forty petitions” sounds like a finding one can carry from an inquiry into participation to an inquiry into organization. In fact it fits neither inquiry particularly well until someone explains what those forty units were.

The archive eventually added two switches to its search. A reader could group results by physical sheet or by named participant, and could see the grouping used in a downloaded table. The archivists resisted adding a button labeled “best estimate.” Had a visitor asked for the best estimate of anything in particular, they could have helped. Their refusal was directed at the curious idea that the purpose of an estimate could be supplied after the estimate itself.

Which claim is most central to the passage?
Choices:
A physical sheet is the most reliable unit for reconstructing collective political effort.
A historical count becomes interpretable when its unit is matched to the question being asked.
Text searches generally distort evidence more than the impressions of a historian who reads entire files.
Archives can solve most disputes over interpretation by giving readers access to original images.
Answer: A historical count becomes interpretable when its unit is matched to the question being asked.
Reason: The competing counts preserve different information. The author endorses counting while insisting on an explicit purpose and unit.
Source: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/prepare-mcat-exam/whats-mcat-exam-pdf-outline

One proposed remedy was to count signatures. A hundred names, on this view, ought to carry the same weight whether they arrived on one sheet or a hundred. That seems fair if the historian wants to know how many people were willing to put their names to a demand. But a signature gathered during a shift change could take seconds, while delivering a petition to the council might cost a day’s wages. A signature count retains an answer about participation while discarding evidence about the work of organizing it. The two streets might have differed most in precisely that respect.

A second remedy was to preserve photographs of every sheet. The photographs were welcome. One showed that what looked in transcription like a second signer was a witness attesting to the mark of someone who could not write. Yet photographs do little for the reader who is first deciding which street to investigate. That reader still encounters a list produced by choices about what counts as a document. A picture can correct a conclusion once the reader has found it. It cannot, by itself, tell the reader which pictures the search failed to bring together.

There was a further difficulty. A husband and wife sometimes signed one sheet under the name of their shop. Counting the sheet was easy. Counting the names meant deciding whether the couple, the shop, or the person who held the pen had made the demand. Even the apparently modest unit of a participant already contained an interpretation.

Some archivists took this argument as an objection to counting. Far from it. If no one counts anything, a street represented by one eloquent letter may fill half a chapter while a street represented by forty terse petitions gets a sentence. The discipline of counting can expose that imbalance. The difficulty begins when the count is allowed to travel without its question. “Forty petitions” sounds like a finding one can carry from an inquiry into participation to an inquiry into organization. In fact it fits neither inquiry particularly well until someone explains what those forty units were.

The archive eventually added two switches to its search. A reader could group results by physical sheet or by named participant, and could see the grouping used in a downloaded table. The archivists resisted adding a button labeled “best estimate.” Had a visitor asked for the best estimate of anything in particular, they could have helped. Their refusal was directed at the curious idea that the purpose of an estimate could be supplied after the estimate itself.

Suppose the archive retained both search switches but stopped labeling which grouping was used in downloaded tables. Which concern would remain most directly unresolved?
Choices:
The original sheets would gradually become inaccessible to volunteers.
Readers could no longer correct the spelling of names using photographs.
The names of people who signed printed petitions would disappear.
Another analyst might reuse a count without knowing what its units represented.
Answer: Another analyst might reuse a count without knowing what its units represented.
Reason: The recorded grouping preserves the meaning of a count when it leaves the search interface.
Source: Original passage and item · AAMC CARS framework · https://students-residents.aamc.org/prepare-mcat-exam/whats-mcat-exam-pdf-outline
